items.stem: Evaluate $\dfrac{2+3}{3}+\dfrac{4}{2+2}$ and give the result as a single fraction.
items.hint: A fraction bar groups everything above it and everything below it, so finish each of those little sums before you divide or combine anything.
worked: The bar groups the whole numerator: $\dfrac{2+3}{3}=\dfrac{5}{3}$.
It groups the whole denominator too: $\dfrac{4}{2+2}=\dfrac{4}{4}=1$.

items.stem: Exactly one of the following four statements is true. Which one is it?
items.hint: Turn each side of a statement you doubt into a single fraction; one honest number check is enough to kill three of these.
worked: Dividing flips the second fraction: $\dfrac{3}{5}\div\dfrac{9}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}\cdot\dfrac{10}{9}=\dfrac{30}{45}=\dfrac{2}{3}$, so that statement is true.
$\dfrac{1}{2+3}=\dfrac{1}{5}$, but $\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{3}=\dfrac{5}{6}$: a sum on the bottom never splits.
$\dfrac{7+4}{4}=\dfrac{11}{4}$, not $7$: only a whole factor cancels, never one piece of a sum.

items.stem: A student evaluates $\dfrac{8}{2+2}-\left(\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and writes $\dfrac{8}{2}+\dfrac{8}{2}-\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{27}{4}$. Two separate rules were broken. What is the correct value?
items.hint: Repair one rule at a time: a sum underneath the bar must be finished before you divide, and the minus in front of the bracket reaches both terms inside it.
worked: Finish the denominator first: $\dfrac{8}{2+2}=\dfrac{8}{4}=2$, so splitting it into $\dfrac{8}{2}+\dfrac{8}{2}$ was the first broken rule.
The minus reaches both terms, so the bracket must be finished first: $\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{3}{4}-\dfrac{2}{4}=\dfrac{1}{4}$.
